title: Q-LCAN: Anatomy-Constrained Quantum-Agentic Systems for MRI-Derived Structural Surgical Digital Twins in Uterine Adenomyosis.
abstract: Accurate patient-specific structural assessment of adenomyosis is essential for fertility-preserving treatment planning, but pelvic T2-weighted MRI is difficult to parse because the uterus, endometrium, ectopic glands, hemorrhagic foci, and adenomyoma are nested, overlapping, and highly imbalanced. We propose Q-LCAN, an anatomy-constrained Quantum-Agentic System that converts MRI into a structured surgical digital twin. A dense 3D decoder first estimates target-specific probability maps and signed distance fields. Five target agents then exchange visual evidence under predefined anatomical axioms, while quantum-enhanced differentiable action projection (Q-DAP) calibrates restricted expand, shrink, or hold actions before vision-language level-set control. A detached anatomical correction module and an independent audit reduce and report residual violations. On 658 multicenter examinations, Q-LCAN achieved case-level five-target macro-average DSC/ASSD of 0.814/2.23 mm in internal five-fold validation and 0.802/2.33 mm in external testing. Compared with the strongest protocol-aligned baseline, Q-LCAN improved macro DSC by 0.018 and 0.019 and reduced ASSD by 0.29 and 0.31 mm, with gains concentrated in ectopic glands, hemorrhagic foci, adenomyoma burden, lesion-to-endometrium distance, residual lesion ratio, and candidate resection-boundary distance. Q-LCAN provides an auditable quantum-agentic framework for MRI-derived structural twins; its millimeter-scale descriptors are intended as preoperative decision support, not autonomous operative guidance.

title: Latent Interpolation Learning Using Diffusion Models for Cardiac Volume Reconstruction.
abstract: Cardiac Magnetic Resonance (CMR) imaging is a critical tool for diagnosing and managing cardiovascular disease, yet its utility is often limited by the sparse acquisition of 2D short-axis slices, resulting in incomplete volumetric information. Accurate 3D reconstruction from these sparse slices is essential for comprehensive cardiac assessment, but existing methods face challenges, including reliance on predefined interpolation schemes (e.g., linear or spherical), computational inefficiency, and dependence on additional semantic inputs such as segmentation labels or motion data. To address these limitations, we propose a novel Cardiac Latent Interpolation Diffusion (CaLID) framework that introduces three key innovations. First, we present a data-driven interpolation scheme based on diffusion models, which can capture complex, non-linear relationships between sparse slices and improves reconstruction accuracy. Second, we design a computationally efficient method that operates in the latent space and speeds up generative 3D whole-heart upsampling time by a factor of 24, reducing computational overhead compared to previous methods. Third, with only sparse 2D CMR images as input, our method achieves SOTA performance against baseline methods, eliminating the need for auxiliary input such as morphological guidance, thus simplifying workflows. We further extend our method to 2D+T data, enabling the effective modeling of spatiotemporal dynamics and ensuring temporal coherence. Extensive volumetric evaluations and downstream segmentation tasks demonstrate that CaLID achieves superior reconstruction quality and efficiency. By addressing the fundamental limitations of existing approaches, our framework advances the state of the art for spatio and spatiotemporal whole-heart reconstruction, offering a robust and clinically practical solution for cardiovascular imaging. The code is available at https://github.com/niklasbubeck/calid.

title: Can Simple MRI Characteristics Predict Molecular Subgroups in Paediatric Medulloblastoma?
abstract: Introduction Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant paediatric central nervous system (CNS) tumour and is classified using molecular subgroups: WNT, SHH and non-WNT/non-SHH. Subgroup identification guides prognosis and treatment, but requires molecular testing, which is not universally available. MRI is routine in assessment of CNS tumours, and the MRI characteristics may serve as surrogate markers for medulloblastoma subgrouping. This study aims to use simple MRI surrogate markers identified by Perreault et al., against local medulloblastoma cases and their final molecular outcome. Method Retrospective cohort study of paediatric medulloblastomas at a single tertiary children's hospital between January 2015 and October 2025. MRI studies were reviewed by a paediatric neuroradiologist and a radiology registrar in consensus. Tumours were classified by location (cerebellar hemisphere, cerebellopontine angle/cerebellar peduncle (CP/CPA), or midline/fourth ventricle) and enhancement pattern (minimal/none = < 10%, heterogeneous = 10%-90%, solid = > 90%). Associations between MRI features and molecular subgroup were assessed. Results Twenty-two cases were analysed: SHH 22.7% (5/22), WNT 13.6% (3/22) and non-WNT/non-SHH 63.7% (14/22). Most tumours were midline (90.9%), with two hemispheric lesions and no CP/CPA. Enhancement patterns were heterogeneous (54.5%), solid (36.4%) and minimal/none (9.1%). Hemispheric location was associated with SHH tumours (p = 0.043), and all WNT tumours demonstrated solid enhancement (p = 0.036). No other statistically significant associations were identified. Conclusion MRI characteristics offer promising surrogate markers for medulloblastoma subtype. The only strong predictor we found corresponding with Perreault et al. is that hemispheric lesions are correlated with SHH-activated medulloblastoma. This supports further investigation of MRI markers as non-invasive and preoperative medulloblastoma subgroup prediction.

title: Radiographic measurements of cardiac silhouette and skeletal landmarks in companion galahs (Eolophus roseicapilla) and sulphur-crested cockatoos (Cacatua galerita).
abstract: Introduction Cardiac disease is common in companion birds, yet its diagnosis remains a challenge due to limited validated tests. Radiography is frequently used to assess cardiac size in birds; however, interspecies variation necessitates species-specific reference intervals. This study aimed to establish the cardiac silhouette in companion galahs (Eolophus roseicapilla) and sulphur-crested cockatoos (Cacatua galerita). Methods Ventrodorsal (VD) and laterolateral (LL) radiographs of 30 adult galahs and 21 adult cockatoos were obtained from medical records that were admitted to the University of Queensland Veterinary Teaching Hospital from 2013 to 2023. In the VD view, cardiac width (CW) was measured with other anatomical landmarks including thoracic width (TW), clavicular distance (ClD), coracoid width (CoW) and 3rd-4th rib distance (RD). In the LL view, the cardiac length (CL) was measured and correlated to sternal length (SL). Results Significant positive correlations were found between CW and weight ( ρ=0.777 , p < 0.001); CW and TW ( ρ=0.789 , p < 0.001), in galahs. In cockatoos, significant positive correlations were found between CW and CoW ( ρ=0.541 , p = 0.011); CW and ClD ( ρ=0.491 , p < 0.021). The 25th-75th percentile range (PR) for CW:TW ranged from 52 to 62.5% and 60-65% in cockatoos and galahs, respectively. Conclusion In galahs, CW correlated positively with the TW, and the 25th-75th PR for CW:TW should be 60%-65%. In cockatoos, the CW is better correlated to the CoW and ClD with the 25th-75th PRI of 549.5%-609.5% and 91.5%-103.0% respectively. The cardiac silhouette was larger in galahs than in cockatoos.

The 25th-75th percentile range (PR) for CW:TW ranged from 52 to 62.5% and 60-65% in cockatoos and galahs, respectively.

In galahs, CW correlated positively with the TW, and the 25th-75th PR for CW:TW should be 60%-65%. In cockatoos, the CW is better correlated to the CoW and ClD with the 25th-75th PRI of 549.5%-609.5% and 91.5%-103.0% respectively. The cardiac silhouette was larger in galahs than in cockatoos.

title: Impact of AI-Assisted Endoscopy on Secondary Review and Referral Decisions in Gastric Cancer Screening: A Multicenter Real-World Study.
abstract: Objectives Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted endoscopy may support gastric cancer screening, but its impact on structured secondary human review remains unclear. We evaluated secondary review modifications and referral decisions before and after AI implementation. Methods This retrospective multicenter study included 5013 screening esophagogastroduodenoscopy examinations performed before (n = 2021) and after (n = 2992) AI implementation. The primary outcome was secondary review modifications. Secondary outcomes included referral for further diagnostic evaluation. Multivariable logistic regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, Helicobacter pylori eradication status, prior-year endoscopy, and endoscopist experience were performed. Interaction analyses according to endoscopist experience and inverse probability of treatment weighting analyses were conducted. No external reference standard was available to verify secondary-review modifications or referral decisions. Results Secondary review modifications increased from 1.2% in the pre-AI period to 3.7% in the AI period (p < 0.01). A significant interaction was observed between AI implementation and endoscopist experience (p for interaction < 0.01), with increased modifications primarily among nonexpert endoscopists. Cancer-related modifications remained uncommon but increased after AI implementation (0.6% vs. 0.2%, p = 0.04). Referral rates decreased from 4.9% to 2.8% (p < 0.01), and AI implementation was independently associated with lower odds of referral (adjusted OR = 0.53; 95% confidence interval = 0.36-0.77). Conclusions AI-assisted endoscopy was associated with lower referral rates; however, secondary review modifications persisted after AI implementation, particularly among nonexpert endoscopists. These findings describe workflow changes and do not establish the clinical validity of the modifications or the appropriateness of referral decisions.

title: Multi-Level Automated Classification of Temporomandibular Joint Degenerative Joint Disease on CBCT Using 3D Volumetric and 2D Slice-Based Approaches.
abstract: Background Temporomandibular joint degenerative joint disease (TMJ DJD) causes progressive osseous changes of the mandibular condyle and articular fossa. Although cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) enables detailed assessment, manual interpretation is time-consuming and subject to inter-observer variability. Objectives To develop and validate a multilevel AI framework for CBCT-based TMJ DJD assessment using three-dimensional classification, quantitative volumetric analysis, and two-dimensional slice-based detection. Methods Full-field-of-view CBCT scans from 222 patients were used for three-dimensional analysis. A 3D V-Net classified condyles into Normal, Osteophyte, Erosion, Flattening, and Severe Degeneration categories. Condylar volume was quantitatively compared between TMJ DJD and non-TMJ DJD groups and among degenerative subgroups. For slice-based analysis, 727 temporomandibular joints from 416 patients were retrospectively evaluated. Automated sagittal slice extraction based on the condylion landmark generated 5787 condylar and 666 articular fossa slices. YOLOv10 was used for multi-lesion detection of six condylar and three fossa categories. Results The 3D V-Net achieved an overall sensitivity of 79.47%. Condylar volume differed significantly between TMJ DJD and non-TMJ DJD groups (ANOVA, p = 0.025), whereas differences among the TMJ DJD subgroups were not statistically significant. For condylar slice-based detection, YOLOv10 achieved 94.0% sensitivity, 82.8% precision, 88.0% F1-score, and 91.3% AP@0.50. For articular fossa detection, YOLOv10 achieved 92.41% sensitivity, 83.91% precision, 87.95% F1-score, and 82.01% AP@0.50. Conclusions Three-dimensional AI enabled overall TMJ DJD classification but showed limited discrimination of specific subgroups, particularly erosion. Volumetric analysis differentiated DJD from non-DJD cases but not among DJD subgroups. In contrast, slice-based YOLOv10 effectively detected and labelled specific condylar and fossa degenerative changes, providing more detailed lesion-level characterization.

title: Polarization Sensitive Optical Coherence Tomography for Surgical Margin Assessment for Canine Soft Tissue Sarcoma.
abstract: Soft tissue sarcomas (STSs) and skeletal muscle both appear high scattering on spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) imaging, which resulted in instances of misclassification by observers in prior soft tissue sarcoma margin assessment studies. Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) is an extension of OCT that provides additional information about tissue polarization contrast. In this prospective study we wanted to evaluate whether PS-OCT improves tissue differentiation and diagnostic accuracy compared to spectral-domain OCT (SD-OCT) alone. PS-OCT images from surgical margins of 10 resected STS were compared with histopathology to identify characteristic features of normal and neoplastic tissues. Then, six observers of varying OCT image interpretation experience assessed surgical margins from 30 resected STS using SD-OCT alone and SD-OCT combined with PS-OCT. PS-OCT images demonstrated distinct birefringence (optical patterns), corresponding to tissue organization: skeletal muscle exhibited alternating high and low birefringence bands, fascia showed variable birefringence and STS had uniformly low birefringence. Overall diagnostic accuracy was high for both modalities [correct classification rate: SD-OCT alone 93.7% (95% confidence interval (CI): 90.1, 96.0) vs. SD-OCT combined with PS-OCT 92.6% (95% = CI: 89.3, 95.4)]; adding PS-OCT did not significantly improve accuracy across all observers (p = 0.82), though expert observers benefited significantly (p = 0.0018). Interobserver and intraobserver agreement ranged from substantial to near perfect. These findings suggest PS-OCT can be interpreted reliably after brief training and may enhance accuracy for experienced users. Further research should explore structured training and real-time applications for comprehensive surgical margin evaluation.

title: A New Application of 64 CuCl 2 PET/CT: Imaging of Cats With Mammary Carcinoma.
abstract: Feline mammary carcinoma (FMC) is an aggressive and highly metastatic cancer that shares molecular and clinical characteristics with human triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), making it a relevant comparative model for a disease lacking targeted therapies. This study investigated the feasibility and clinical utility of 64 CuCl 2 PET/CT imaging in cats with naturally occurring mammary carcinoma. Eight cats (seven tumour-bearing, one healthy control) were administered an intravenous dose of 64 CuCl 2 and underwent whole-body PET/CT imaging. Semi-quantitative analysis was performed using standardized uptake values (SUVs), and tumour-to-muscle ratios were calculated to assess lesion conspicuity. Serum ceruloplasmin concentrations were measured as a marker of systemic copper metabolism. All primary masses were 64 Cu-avid and conspicuous, with consistently elevated tumour-to-muscle ratios across tumour-bearing cats, allowing clear differentiation between neoplastic and normal tissue. Imaging provided additional staging information by identifying locally invasive and metastatic disease that was not fully evident on physical examination. Physiologic tracer distribution was characterized by high uptake in the liver and gallbladder and low uptake in skeletal muscle, which served as a reliable reference tissue. Serum ceruloplasmin concentrations varied widely and did not correlate with tumour uptake. These findings suggest that 64 CuCl 2 PET/CT is a feasible functional imaging modality for FMC, potentially aiding in tumour detection. This was an exploratory study, and not all imaging results could be confirmed by cytology or histopathology. Nonetheless, our findings suggest that 64 CuCl 2 PET/CT should be investigated further as a method for probing copper utilization in FMC.

title: Clinical Presentation, Acute Clinical Response, Drug Tolerability, and Short-Term Outcome of Cats Treated for Acute Congestive Heart Failure With Pimobendan (2017-2022): 71 Cases.
abstract: Objective To describe clinical effects, drug tolerability, and short-term outcomes of cats treated with pimobendan (PB) in conjunction with other therapies for acute congestive heart failure (CHF). Design Retrospective single-center study (2017 to 2022). Setting Academic teaching and referral hospital. Animals Seventy-one cats with acute CHF treated with PB and furosemide. Treatment included dobutamine (DB) in 15 cases. Measurements and main results Physical examination results, laboratory results, and radiographic pulmonary infiltrate scoring were assessed in all cats at admission and 24 h later. Respiratory rate and radiographic pulmonary infiltrate scores decreased after 24 h of therapy (p < 0.0001 for both values). Anemia and hypochloremia were more common than azotemia, hyponatremia, and hypokalemia on Day 1. Serum chloride and potassium concentrations decreased, and serum creatinine concentration increased after therapy (p < 0.05), but none of these values was associated with prolonged hospitalization or reduced survival. Cats receiving PB exhibited few adverse clinical signs. Seven of 15 cats (47%) that received concurrent DB therapy were suspected of having adverse effects that responded to decreased dosage or discontinuation of the medication. There was no difference in survival to discharge (p = 0.17) or days of hospitalization (p = 0.78) between cats receiving DB therapy and those that did not. Overall survival to discharge was 76%, and 75% of cats discharged alive were discharged in ≤3 days. Conclusions The short-term prognosis for cats treated for acute CHF was good, and PB therapy appeared to be well tolerated. Most cats showed clinical and radiographic improvement in the first 24 h of therapy and were hospitalized for ≤3 days. The addition of DB to therapy in some cats did not alter survival and was associated with adverse clinical signs in 7/15 cats (47%) treated with DB.

title: Generalized Megaesophagus Concurrent With Toxocariasis in a Cat.
abstract: Feline megaesophagus is a rare disorder characterized by esophageal hypomotility and dilation, resulting in regurgitation, weight loss, and occasionally death. This report describes the clinical and paraclinical findings of generalized megaesophagus with a possible contribution of toxocariasis in a kitten. A 2-month-old female cat was referred with chief complaints of lethargy, hyporexia, dyspnea, and vomiting/regurgitation. Physical examination of the kitten revealed bradycardia, bradypnea, hypothermia, dehydration, and lung crackles. The most notable laboratory results were leukopenia with severe toxic changes in neutrophils. Radiographic findings were compatible with the diagnosis of generalized megaesophagus. Despite supportive measures, the kitten died the next day. Necropsy revealed diffuse esophageal dilation and Toxocara spp. roundworms in the stomach and duodenum. Histopathology showed an ascarid larva in the esophagus, necrosis and metaplasia in the pylorus, and absence of villi and Brunner's glands in the duodenum. Based on the morphological identification of the adult gastrointestinal nematodes, the final diagnosis was generalized megaesophagus of unspecified classification concurrent with toxocariasis. However, the exact cause of death could not be established. Although respiratory abnormalities raised suspicion of a pulmonary complication, pneumonia was not confirmed. We hypothesized that toxocariasis may have contributed to esophageal dysfunction in this kitten through potential mechanisms such as vomiting, gastrointestinal obstruction, or neurological involvement; however, these mechanisms could not be directly demonstrated. Therefore, parasitic diseases, including toxocariasis, may be considered among potential differential diagnoses or contributing conditions in young cats presenting with megaesophagus, particularly when concurrent gastrointestinal parasitism or related complications are identified. Further studies are required to clarify the possible relationship between toxocariasis and esophageal dysfunction.

title: Kidney volumetry for predicting long-term outcome in acute kidney injury: A retrospective cohort study.
abstract: Introduction Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is effective for severe acute kidney injury (AKI); however, predicting successful CRRT discontinuation and long-term outcomes remains challenging. Although urinary neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL) levels and kidney volume measured by computed tomography (CT) have been associated with renal prognosis, it remains unclear whether their combination improves predictive accuracy. This study evaluated whether combining urinary NGAL levels with kidney volume measured by CT improves prediction accuracy. Methods In this retrospective cohort study, urinary NGAL levels and height-adjusted total kidney volume (HtTKV) were assessed for their ability to predict successful CRRT discontinuation and major adverse kidney events at 90 days (MAKE90). Results Among the 74 patients included, CRRT discontinuation was successful in 55 (74.3%), and MAKE90 occurred in 31 (41.9%). Urinary NGAL (area under the curve [AUC], 0.86; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.76-0.95) was a significant predictor of CRRT discontinuation, whereas HtTKV was not. For long-term outcomes, urinary NGAL (AUC, 0.73 [95% CI, 0.61-0.85]) and HtTKV (AUC, 0.67 [95% CI, 0.54-0.80]) were significantly associated with MAKE90. Adding HtTKV to urinary NGAL significantly improved prediction of MAKE90, as demonstrated by reclassification analyses (net reclassification improvement and integrated discrimination improvement). Conclusions Adding HtTKV significantly improved the prediction of long-term MAKE90 based on NGAL levels, but not that of short-term CRRT discontinuation. These findings in this proof-of-concept study suggest that structural kidney assessment by CT volumetry may complement urinary NGAL for long-term risk stratification in patients with severe AKI requiring CRRT.

title: The fetal Ear-Eye and Ear-Rotation angle: A pilot study on novel 3D ultrasound measure-ments for prenatal diagnosis of low-set ears.
abstract: Introduction Low-set ears are frequently associated with chromosomal aberrations, congenital malformations, and genetic syndromes. While typically described postnatally, prenatal diagnosis usually relies on subjective expert pattern recognition. We introduce a standardized 3D ultra-sound measurement approach to assess fetal ear position relative to the eye and head. Methods Retrospective pilot analysis of prospectively acquired 3D head volumes (16-34 weeks; 10/2023-10/2025). The "ear-eye angle," "ear-rotation angle," and ear length were meas-ured by two blinded examiners in healthy controls and a malformation group. Results We included 102 fetuses (82 controls, 20 malformations) at a median 21 weeks' gesta-tion (16-34). The malformation group had a significantly larger median ear-eye angle than con-trols (3.29° [-2.81-7.88] vs. 1.02° [-11.04-8.75]; P<0.001) and median ear-rotation angle (17.50° [-33.75-37.20] vs. 12.10° [0.00-38.40]; P=0.029). Logistic regression showed that for every one-degree increase in the ear-eye angle, the odds of a malformation increased significant-ly (OR 1.36; 95% CI: 1.11-1.65; P = 0.002). ROC analysis revealed the ear-eye angle had supe-rior discriminative ability over the ear-rotation angle (AUC 0.76 vs. 0.66). Inter-observer agree-ment was high (ear-eye ICC=0.96; ear-rotation ICC=0.92). Conclusion Systematic evaluation of the fetal ear on routinely collected 3D volumes is feasible. Both angles were significantly larger in affected fetuses compared to healthy controls. However, due to the limited sample size and prevalence of abnormal cases, these diagnostic performance metrics should be interpreted with caution and require validation in larger cohorts.

title: Post-mortem MRI assessment of fetal corpus callosum growth patterns between 14 and 22 weeks of gestation.
abstract: Introduction The corpus callosum (CC) is the largest commissural tract in the human brain, playing a crucial role in interhemispheric communication and neurodevelopment. Although ultrasonography and MRI have been used to assess callosal morphology, most available data are from later gestational ages, with limited normative information for fetuses below 20 weeks. This study aims to fill this gap by evaluating the biometry of the corpus callosum using high-resolution post-mortem fetal brain MRI between 14 and 22 gestational weeks. Materials and methods This observational cross-sectional study analyzed post-mortem MRI scans of 77 neurotypical fetal brains aged 14-22 gestational weeks. Imaging was performed on a 3T MRI scanner using a dedicated fetal protocol. T2-weighted STIR sequences provided optimal contrast for delineating the corpus callosum. The anteroposterior (AP) length and body thickness were measured on mid-sagittal images. Data were analyzed using SPSS with descriptive statistics, Pearson's correlation, linear regression, and ANOVA at a significance level of p < 0.05. Results The mean AP length of the corpus callosum was 1.78 ± 0.69 cm, and the mean body thickness was 0.171 ± 0.031 cm. AP length showed a strong positive correlation with gestational age (r = 0.952, p < 0.001), while body thickness showed a moderate correlation (r = 0.613, p < 0.001). Conclusion This study provides early normative post-mortem MRI data of corpus callosum growth between 14 and 22 weeks. The findings establish reference values that may assist in early detection of callosal dysgenesis and related neurodevelopmental abnormalities.

title: Calcium Overload in Trisomy 21: An Underrecognized Cause of Persistent Hypercalcaemia - A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Calcium overload in trisomy 21 is a rare and underrecognized cause of persistent parathyroid hormone (PTH)-independent hypercalcaemia in infants and young children with Down syndrome. Characteristic features include hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis, renal impairment, and failure to thrive. Delayed recognition may result in avoidable long-term complications. Case presentation A 21-month-old boy with trisomy 21 presented with a six-month history of recurrent vomiting, feeding difficulties, and failure to thrive. Bilateral nephrocalcinosis was detected incidentally on abdominal ultrasound. Laboratory evaluation revealed marked hypercalcaemia with suppressed PTH and 1,25(OH)₂D, hypercalciuria, and acute kidney injury. Extensive diagnostic work-up excluded alternative causes of PTH-independent hypercalcaemia. Nutritional assessment showed an almost exclusively milk-based diet with minimal solid food intake. Initial treatment with intravenous fluids and a single dose of pamidronate resulted in only transient improvement. Following the diagnosis of calcium overload, a calcium-restricted diet consisting of normal and low-calcium formula was introduced and adjusted according to biochemical response. Serum calcium normalized and remained stable throughout 11 months of follow-up. Growth and developmental progress improved, while nephrocalcinosis persisted and renal function partially recovered. Conclusion Calcium overload in trisomy 21 should be considered in young children with Down syndrome presenting with failure to thrive, recurrent vomiting, and nephrocalcinosis in combination with PTH-independent hypercalcemia. Early recognition and initiation of dietary calcium restriction may prevent long-term complications such as chronic kidney disease and prolonged growth impairment.

title: Diagnosis and treatment of urothelial carcinoma of the upper urinary tract: Evaluation of guideline compliance 2011-2024.
abstract: Background Urothelial carcinoma of the upper urinary tract (UTUC) requires a complex, multimodal treatment approach. The European Association of Urology (EAU) publishes evidence-based guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of this rare tumour every year. However, due to the low number of cases and diagnostic challenges, their implementation in everyday clinical practice is often difficult. The objective of this retrospective analysis was to evaluate guideline-compliant care for patients diagnosed with UTUC and to investigate potential associations between non-guideline therapy decisions and overall survival and other oncological outcomes. Methods The study included 181 patients diagnosed with UTUC who were treated at our clinic between 2011 and 2024. Treatment courses and oncological outcomes were analyzed based on EAU guidelines, and the overall course was examined in relation to treatment adherence. Results 13% (n=25) of patients received diagnostics or therapy that did not comply with guidelines. The main causes were a lack of resection of the bladder cuff (n=13; 52%), the absence of adjuvant chemotherapy (n=8, 32% 2020 - 2024), the absence of an interdisciplinary case discussion in the form of a tumour board (n=3; 17%), and inadequate surgical treatment (n=1; 5%). In unadjusted analyses, omission of bladder cuff resection was associated with poorer overall survival (p=0.047) and a higher recurrence rate (p=0.038), while the association with overall survival was no longer statistically significant in an exploratory analysis adjusted for age and pathological tumour stage (HR 0.57, 95% CI 0.25-1.30; p=0.183). In addition, diagnostics, the interpretation of CT, cytology and URS biopsy results for the correct classification of low-risk and high-risk patients, and the administration of adjuvant chemotherapy repeatedly showed deviations from the guideline-based criteria for risk stratification. Conclusion Despite clear recommendations from the EAU, consistent implementation in everyday clinical practice remains a challenge. In addition to the rarity of the condition, challenging diagnostic pathways contribute to its limited use. However, guideline-compliant care may be of clinical importance, as deviations could be associated with poorer oncological outcomes.

title: AI and Deep Learning in Cardiovascular Imaging: From Risk Stratification to Precision Phenotyping.
abstract: Cardiovascular imaging plays a central role in the diagnosis, risk stratification, and management of cardiovascular disease, yet the complexity and volume of imaging data increasingly exceed the capacity of conventional interpretation. Artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning offer new tools to extract quantitative, prognostic, and phenotypic information from routine cardiovascular images. This review summarizes the fundamentals of AI and deep learning, including model architectures, training strategies, and their relevance to cardiovascular imaging, followed by a focused discussion of current applications across chest radiography, chest computed tomography, computed tomography angiography/cardiac computed tomography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, echocardiography, and nuclear cardiology imaging. Studies were selected with emphasis on original investigations, large cohort analyses, and external validation studies reflecting current applications of AI in cardiovascular risk stratification and precision phenotyping. Across these modalities, AI applications in automated image processing and analysis have become relatively mature. Multiple multicenter and real-world studies have validated their value in improving efficiency and supporting cardiovascular management. Approaches that move beyond conventional human-defined imaging metrics to infer cardiovascular risk and disease phenotype remain at an earlier stage, requiring further standardization, validation, and clinical evaluation. AI is expanding the role of cardiovascular imaging from visual interpretation toward integrated assessment for risk stratification and precision phenotyping, though further work is needed to confirm generalizability and real-world performance before these tools can guide individual patient management.

title: GFC-Unet: An optimized 3D U-Net-based method for brain tumor segmentation.
abstract: Accurate brain tumor segmentation is critical for diagnosis and treatment planning. However, U-Net-based models struggle with complex tumor morphologies and fine boundaries. This paper proposes a novel brain tumor segmentation network, termed GFC-Unet. Built upon the 3D U-Net architecture, this network introduces three core modules: (1) the Multi-modal Feature Recalibration (MFR) module; (2) the Gated Feature Convolution (GFC) module; and (3) the Feature Uncertainty Evaluation (FUE) module. Experimental results on the Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS) 2020 and 2021 datasets demonstrate that GFC-Unet achieves Dice coefficients of 92.82%, 87.74%, and 87.47% on BraTS2020, and 92.61%, 87.49%, and 86.89% on BraTS2021 for whole tumor (WT), tumor core (TC), and enhancing tumor (ET), respectively. Ablation studies validate the effectiveness of each module. Furthermore, extended experiments on the Data Science Bowl (DSB) 2018 cell nucleus segmentation and International Skin Imaging Collaboration (ISIC) 2018 skin lesion segmentation tasks demonstrate the strong generalization capability. By integrating these modules, GFC-Unet improves segmentation accuracy and boundary delineation, demonstrating promise for supporting clinical decision-making.

title: Breast cancer overdiagnosis due to mammography screening-A long-term follow-up population study of BreastScreen Norway.
abstract: ObjectivesEstimates of breast cancer overdiagnosis related to mammography screening vary substantially. Overdiagnosis is commonly defined as cases that would not have been detected during the person's remaining lifetime in the absence of screening. We here aim to quantify overdiagnosis in the population-based BreastScreen Norway mammography screening program using long-term follow-up and more detailed modeling than previous studies.SettingWe applied data on Norwegian screening patterns and breast carcinoma incidence for the period 1987-2019, covering women aged 49-84, leveraging the gradual implementation of the organized biennial BreastScreen Norway screening program for women aged 50-69 during 1995-2005.MethodsUsing an extended age-period-cohort model, we estimated excess lifetime risk of invasive breast cancer and ductal carcinoma in situ in the presence of program screening, as an indicator of overdiagnosis among screen-detected cases.ResultsLifetime risk of breast carcinomas was 6.6% (95% confidence interval: 2.5%-10.7%) higher for invited than for non-invited women. This indicates that 18% (95% confidence interval: 7.3%-28.0%) of screen-detected cases may be overdiagnosed, and that approximately one in 86 (95% confidence interval: 54-210) screened women were overdiagnosed during their screening period. title: Silent Hypoxemia in High-Altitude Pulmonary Edema: A Case Report.
abstract: We report a case of a trekker who ascended to Tilicho Lake (4919 m) from Kathmandu (1400 m) in 3 days. On day 3, he descended to Shree Kharka (4045 m). The following day, he trekked to Yak Kharka (4025 m) where, although he had no symptoms, he measured his own oxygen saturation (SpO 2 ) at 72% in ambient air. Overnight, his SpO 2 ranged from 75-80% on oxygen 2L/min via nasal cannula. The next day his SpO 2 dropped to 47% while still on oxygen. He descended on horseback to Manang (3500 m), where his SpO 2 was 70% on room air. He was diagnosed with high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE). He was treated with oxygen, 4L by nasal cannula, and nifedipine. The following day, he flew to Kathmandu, where he made a full recovery. Trekkers may develop life-threatening HAPE without obvious symptoms or signs. Slow ascent can decrease the likelihood of developing HAPE, but trekkers do not always follow the recommended ascent rate. Early detection, by history and physical examination and with point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS), if available, is critical in resource-limited regions such as ours. The keys to managing HAPE are early recognition and management, including descending to a lower altitude as soon as possible.

title: Prognosis and treatment-related toxicities in Down syndrome acute lymphoblastic leukemia in JCCG ALL-B12.
abstract: Children with Down syndrome (DS) have an increased risk of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). Although recent reports describe some improvement, survival in DS-ALL remains inferior to that of non-DS-ALL. This study evaluated the prognosis, relapse patterns, and treatment-related toxicities of DS-ALL in the Japan Children's Cancer Group ALL-B12 trial, a nationwide prospective study using risk-adapted therapy. A total of 1,804 patients, including 44 DS-ALL, were analyzed. Risk classification used standardized criteria. The 5-year event-free survival and overall survival in DS-ALL were 70.5% and 81.8%, respectively, lower than 85.6% and 94.6% in non-DS-ALL (P < 0.001). Survival differences were most pronounced in standard-risk patients. DS-ALL showed fewer favorable genetics and relapse patterns dominated by isolated bone marrow events, with no CNS relapse. CRLF2 rearrangement was assessable in 43 of 44 DS-ALL cases; 15 of 43 (34.9%) were positive. In an exploratory analysis excluding canonical favorable or unfavorable subtypes (n = 36), the 5-year EFS in DS-ALL with and without CRLF2 rearrangement were 57.1% and 81.8%, respectively (P = 0.300), and the corresponding 5-year OS were 78.6% and 86.4%, respectively (P = 0.331). Treatment-related toxicities were more frequent in DS-ALL, including mucositis (27.3% vs. 7.1%), hyperglycemia (25.0% vs. 6.9%), and pulmonary infections (20.5% vs. 7.4%). Among DS-ALL patients with TP2 MRD ≥ 10-4 (n = 3), all relapsed and died within three years. No treatment-related death was recorded after induction, but one death of undetermined cause occurred. These findings highlight the continuing need to optimize DS-ALL therapy to reduce relapse and toxicity. UMIN CT Registry (UMIN000009339) and JCT (jRCTs041180101).

title: Late enhancement and washout maps for distinguishing tumor progression from radiation necrosis in malignant brain tumors: an exploratory study.
abstract: Background Distinguishing between tumor progression and radiation necrosis during brain tumor follow-up is challenging. Advanced MR imaging techniques, such as perfusion, diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), and spectroscopy, can help differentiate between these conditions. In our clinic, we established a novel technique, the rapid washout and late-enhancement map. This study investigated the value of this map in distinguishing true progression from radiation necrosis. Methods Patients with a histologically confirmed initial diagnosis of glioblastoma, high-grade astrocytoma, primary central nervous system lymphoma, or brain metastasis who were undergoing radiochemotherapy and participated in our MRI protocol, including MR perfusion and rapid washout imaging, between January 1, 2024, and December 31, 2025, were included in the study. We volumetrically measured late enhancement and washout in brain tumors at all follow-up examinations and analyzed the resulting volumes. Additionally, we evaluated diffusion-weighted imaging and MR perfusion images. Results A total of 33 patients (25 with glioblastoma, two with astrocytoma grade 4, two with astrocytoma grade 3, one with CNS lymphoma, and three with brain metastasis) were included. Diagnostic confirmation was obtained by histopathological assessment in 20 patients, MRI follow-up in 13 patients, with additional fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography in two. Among these patients, 23 were diagnosed with tumor recurrence, four with mixed pathology comprising "radiation necrosis with scattered active tumor cells", and six with radiation necrosis. The mean washout ratio (± standard deviation) was 31 ± 18 % for progressive disease, 35 ± 20 % for mixed pathology, and 10 ± 7 % for radiation necrosis, respectively. Conclusions The washout ratio can enhance the differentiation between recurrent tumor growth and radiation necrosis during post-treatment monitoring of malignant brain tumors. As MR perfusion can yield inconclusive results in this setting, the proposed method offers complementary information that supports initial diagnostic decision making. Diagnostic discrimination may be strengthened by combining the relative cerebral blood volume with washout ratio analysis, rather than relying on a single imaging marker.

title: Functional and Structural Imaging Features of Cognitive Profiles in Multiple Sclerosis.
abstract: Background and objectives Cognitive impairment affects 40%-70% of patients with multiple sclerosis (MS). Although recent hypothesis-driven and data-driven efforts have identified cognitive phenotypes, functional substrates underlying impairment in such phenotypes are still not clear. Our objective was to identify distinct cognitive phenotypes using clustering in a large cohort of patients with MS and characterize their associated clinical, structural MRI, and resting-state (RS) functional connectivity (FC) features. Methods We conducted an observational, cross-sectional study with right-handed patients with MS and age-matched and sex-matched healthy controls (HCs) who underwent neurologic and neuropsychological evaluation (Brief Repeatable Battery of Neuropsychological tests). Latent profile analysis on cognitive test Z-scores identified MS cognitive phenotypes. 3.0T MRI was used to derive atrophy measures and RS FC within default mode network (DMN I/II), executive control network (ECN), left/right fronto-parietal, language, and salience networks. Linear regression models compared structural MRI and RS FC across cognitive phenotypes and HCs, while polynomial contrasts assessed RS FC patterns across groups. Results Three hundred and sixty-nine patients with MS and 168 HCs were enrolled. Four cognitive phenotypes were detected: preserved cognition ([PC], n = 67[18.2%]), mild single-domain verbal fluency involvement (MSD-VF, n = 37[10.0%]), mild single-domain attention involvement (MSD-A, n = 197[53.4%]), and severe multidomain (SMD) involvement (SMD, n = 68[18.4%]). At corrected threshold, PC patients showed decreased deep gray matter (GM) volumes ( p < 0.001-0.001) and similar RS FC vs HCs, whereas MSD-VF exhibited no significant atrophy and no differences in RS FC vs HCs. MSD-A displayed lower cortical/deep GM volumes vs HCs ( p < 0.001-0.005), whereas SMD had worse clinical and atrophy features ( p < 0.001-0.04), as well as decreased DMN II RS FC ( p = 0.01-0.04) vs other groups. Polynomial contrast analyses revealed significant quadratic patterns with increased RS FC in MSD-VF vs HC/PC groups, followed by decrease in MSD-A and SMD, within DMN II ( p = 0.005), ECN ( p = 0.005), and language network ( p < 0.001). Discussion PC exhibited intact RS FC, whereas SMD presented widespread structural and DMN RS FC damage. These findings advance our understanding of cognitive heterogeneity in MS by revealing distinct structural and functional neuroimaging profiles across cognitive phenotypes, encouraging future longitudinal and multimodal investigations to improve disease characterization and prognostic stratification.

title: Spinal Cord and Nerve Root Involvement in Histiocytic Neoplasms: A Retrospective Observational Cohort Study.
abstract: Background and objectives Histiocytic neoplasms, including Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD), Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH), and Rosai-Dorfman-Destombes disease (RDD), have frequent nervous system involvement. The aim of this study was to characterize the neurologic, radiologic, and laboratory features of spinal cord and nerve root involvement in histiocytic neoplasms. Methods We evaluated patients with biopsy-proven ECD, LCH, or RDD seen at a tertiary referral center between January 1996 and December 2024. Patients were included if spinal MRI demonstrated spinal cord or nerve root involvement. Spinal MRI was performed for evaluation of myelopathic or radicular symptoms or as part of staging in patients with CNS involvement. We collected demographic variables, neurologic syndromes and imaging patterns, treatment characteristics, and outcomes including disability (Expanded Disability Status Scale [EDSS] score) and ambulatory status. The primary outcome was neurologic disability at nadir and last follow-up; secondary outcomes included radiographic patterns and clinical response to treatment. Data were summarized descriptively, with exploratory group comparisons performed using parametric or nonparametric tests as appropriate. Results Among 415 patients with ECD (n = 183), LCH (n = 144), or RDD (n = 88), spinal cord or nerve root involvement was identified in 42 (ECD, 27; LCH, 4; RDD, 11). The median age at onset was 43.1 years (interquartile range 32.1-58.5), and 18 (43%) were female. Most cases were symptomatic (36/42, 86%), with myelopathy as the first neurologic manifestation in 26 (72%). Parenchymal infiltration predominated in the ECD group (17/27, 63%), compared with LCH (2/4, 50%) and RDD (2/11, 18%) groups (Fisher exact test across groups, p = 0.035). Root involvement was more frequent in the RDD group (8/11, 73%) than in the ECD (7/27, 26%) or LCH (1/4, 25%) group (Fisher exact test across groups, p = 0.021). The median EDSS score at nadir was 4.0; 43% required ambulatory aid or worse. After treatment, 22 of 36 symptomatic patients (61%) improved clinically and radiographically, more often in RDD (10/11, 91%) and LCH (2/3, 67%) groups than in the ECD group (10/22, 46%; Fisher exact test across groups, p = 0.022). At a median 5.8-year follow-up, 8 of 38 survivors (21%) required ambulatory assistance or were nonambulatory. Discussion Spinal cord and nerve root involvement occurs in histiocytic neoplasms. These findings support prioritizing spinal MRI in patients with neurologic symptoms or high-risk disease features because early identification may inform diagnosis and management.

The median age at onset was 43.1 years (interquartile range 32.1-58.5), and 18 (43%) were female. Most cases were symptomatic (36/42, 86%), with myelopathy as the first neurologic manifestation in 26 (72%). Parenchymal infiltration predominated in the ECD group (17/27, 63%), compared with LCH (2/4, 50%) and RDD (2/11, 18%) groups (Fisher exact test across groups, p = 0.035). Root involvement was more frequent in the RDD group (8/11, 73%) than in the ECD (7/27, 26%) or LCH (1/4, 25%) group (Fisher exact test across groups, p = 0.021). The median EDSS score at nadir was 4.0; 43% required ambulatory aid or worse. After treatment, 22 of 36 symptomatic patients (61%) improved clinically and radiographically, more often in RDD (10/11, 91%) and LCH (2/3, 67%) groups than in the ECD group (10/22, 46%; Fisher exact test across groups, p = 0.022). At a median 5.8-year follow-up, 8 of 38 survivors (21%) required ambulatory assistance or were nonambulatory.

Discussion

Spinal cord and nerve root involvement occurs in histiocytic neoplasms. These findings support prioritizing spinal MRI in patients with neurologic symptoms or high-risk disease features because early identification may inform diagnosis and management.

title: Behind the Sella: A Rare Case of Pituicytoma Mimicking a Pituitary Adenoma.
abstract: BACKGROUND Pituicytoma is a rare central nervous system (CNS) World Health Organization (WHO) grade I glioma originating from pituicytes, the specialized glial cells of the neurohypophysis or infundibulum. It accounts for less than 0.1% of all sellar and suprasellar masses and often presents a diagnostic challenge because of its clinical and radiological resemblance to other pituitary lesions. CASE REPORT A 48-year-old man was admitted to the endocrinology clinic because of clinical symptoms of hypogonadism, headaches, and visual field defects. Hormonal evaluation revealed hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and hyperprolactinemia. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a sellar-suprasellar mass, initially suggestive of prolactinoma. Lack of response to initial hormone replacement therapy, progressive tumor enlargement, and worsening visual impairment, prompted surgical resection via a right-temporal craniotomy. Histopathological and immunohistochemical examination established the diagnosis of pituicytoma (CNS WHO Grade 1). The postoperative course was complicated by transient cognitive impairment and endocrine deficiencies requiring long-term hormonal replacement therapy. We also review the epidemiology, clinical presentation, and current therapeutic approaches for this uncommon tumor. CONCLUSIONS Pituicytoma is a rare benign tumor that may closely mimic pituitary adenoma, both clinically and radiologically. Clinical manifestations are non-specific and primarily reflect tumor size and local extension. MRI findings are not pathognomic, making histopathological confirmation essential. Surgical resection remains the treatment of choice, whereas radiotherapy may be considered after subtotal resection. The case underscores the importance of recognizing hyperprolactinemia secondary to pituitary stalk compression, careful endocrine interpretation, individualized surgical planning, and prolonged multidisciplinary follow-up, given the uncertain long-term prognosis and potential endocrine sequelae.

title: Primary Intermammary Breast Carcinoma Presenting With Direct Sternal Invasion: A Diagnostic Pitfall of Standard Screening Mammography.
abstract: BACKGROUND Standard screening mammogram views focus on the lateral and posterior breast tissues; the view that best visualizes the intermammary area, the 90-degree lateral or cleavage view, is not typically performed. The limited field of view of mammogram increases the importance of additional imaging with CT, ultrasound, and MRI as a tool in diagnosing neoplasm in the intermammary area. To date, intermammary primary breast carcinoma has been reported only a few times in the literature, and none of these described direct sternal invasion at presentation. CASE REPORT An 85-year-old woman with a past medical history of follicular non-Hodgkin lymphoma treated with bendamustine-rituximab in 2017 (without chest radiation) and significant family history of breast cancer presented to our clinic 2 months after noticing a hard, non-tender nodule on her sternum. She had undergone a routine screening mammogram 8 months prior, which was unremarkable. Subsequent diagnostic workup including targeted ultrasound, and PET-CT identified a hypermetabolic presternal mass. Notably, diagnostic mammography 8 months after the initial screening mammogram also failed to properly visualize the lesion. Biopsy confirmed ER+/PR+, HER2- adenocarcinoma consistent with breast origin. Despite negative initial staging for distant metastasis, pathological examination after resection revealed direct invasion into the sternum, necessitating partial sternectomy. CONCLUSIONS This case highlights a rare intermammary presentation of breast carcinoma with direct sternal invasion, a feature not previously reported. It emphasizes the blind spot of standard screening mammography in the medial breast/cleavage area and the necessity of targeted imaging for palpable parasternal masses, even in the setting of recent negative screens.

title: Skull base osteomyelitis (Necrotising otitis externa) following temporal bone resection and flap reconstruction.
abstract: Necrotising otitis externa (NOE) is a life-threatening infection of the external auditory canal with skull base involvement. We report a case of Citrobacter koseri skull base osteomyelitis with NOE-like features, presenting three months following skull base surgery. A 69-year-old man underwent a left lateral temporal bone resection and pinnectomy with thoracodorsal artery perforator flap reconstruction for extensive basal cell carcinoma. Interval computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated enhancement deep to the flap with skull base and nasopharyngeal involvement, raising concern for recurrence. A postnasal space biopsy excluded malignancy, but cultures isolated C. koseri . Following multidisciplinary review, NOE was diagnosed, and oral cotrimoxazole was initiated, with clinical and radiological improvement. This case highlights the challenges in diagnosing postoperative infection after complex skull-base reconstruction.

title: Evaluation of prenatal genetic aberrations in fetuses with gallbladder abnormalities: A retrospective cohort study.
abstract: Background With the widespread application of chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) in prenatal diagnosis, fetal gallbladder abnormalities have been found to be associated not only with chromosomal aneuploidies but also with certain syndromes caused by submicroscopic chromosomal structural variants. This study aimed to investigate the molecular etiology of fetal gallbladder abnormalities and to provide additional evidence for clinical screening and genetic counseling regarding these anomalies. Material and methods This retrospective study included 258 fetuses diagnosed with gallbladder abnormalities through prenatal ultrasonographic screening. Among these, 167 cases underwent both karyotype analysis and CMA, 14 cases received CMA only, and 77 cases underwent karyotype analysis only. The fetuses were categorized into two groups based on the presence of additional structural anomalies: isolated gallbladder abnormalities (Group A), gallbladder abnormalities accompanied by soft markers (Group B) and gallbladder abnormalities accompanied by structural anomalies or other abnormalities (Group C). Within each of the three groups, cases were further subdivided into subgroups A1/B1/C1, A2/B2/C2, A3/B3/C3, and A4/B4/C4, corresponding to fetuses with nonvisualized gallbladder, gallbladder enlargement, small gallbladder, and other gallbladder abnormalities, respectively. Results Among the total of 258 fetuses, karyotyping identified chromosomal abnormalities in 10 cases (4.2%, 10/240), whereas SNP-array detected abnormalities in 16 cases (8.7%, 16/184). The detection rate of SNP-array was higher than that of traditional chromosome karyotype analysis, and SNP-array identified submicroscopic abnormalities in 7 additional cases that were undetectable by karyotyping. The overall detection rates were significantly higher in gallbladder abnormalities accompanied by structural anomalies or other abnormalities group than that in the isolated gallbladder abnormalities group and gallbladder anomalies accompanied by soft ultrasound markers group(P < 0.05). The highest frequency of chromosomal abnormalities was observed in fetuses presenting with both gallbladder and facial abnormalities. Conclusion For fetuses with gallbladder abnormalities, prenatal genetic diagnosis is recommended, with chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) as the preferred testing method. It can improve the detection rate of chromosomal abnormalities associated with fetal gallbladder abnormalities and identify submicroscopic chromosomal structural variants that conventional karyotyping may miss.

title: Multi-feature Response Attention Network for kidney stone detection and measurement of stone size in ultrasound images.
abstract: Kidney stones are hard deposits formed in the urinary tract due to excess waste and low fluid intake, causing severe abdominal pain. Ultrasound-based kidney stone detection involves identifying and locating stones in the kidneys using high-frequency sound waves to visualize renal structures. Measuring stone size is crucial for early treatment and preventing infection. However, detection is challenging because ultrasound images suffer from noise, lower contrast, and variable quality. To overcome these limitations, the Multi-feature Response Attention Network (MFRANet) is proposed to detect kidney stones. Initially, the input image is allowed for image denoising and edge preservation using Windowed Variation Kernel Wiener Filter (WV-KWF). Further, the kidney region is segmented by the Fuzzy Clustering algorithm with Variable Multi-pixel Fitting spatial information (FCM-VMF). Moreover, descriptor computation is processed by rotated Binary Robust Independent Elementary Feature (rBRIEF) with Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT). Afterwards, the kidney stone is detected using MFRANet, wherein MFRANet is designed by combining Multi-feature Multi-Attention Network (MFMANet), along with Group Response Attention Network (GRA-Net). Next, the detected stone is segmented using Optimized DA-TransUNet (O-DAT), and lastly, the kidney stone size is measured. Performance of the proposed MFRANet is assessed with Accuracy, F1-score, Precision, and True Positive Rate (TPR) which achieved superior values of 96.64%, 96.65%, 97.44%, 95.88% Response Attention Network, Multi-feature Multi-Attention Network, Optimized DA-TransUNet.

title: Coronary microvascular dysfunction in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Background Coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD) is a complication of severe aortic stenosis. Its prevalence after transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) and prognostic significance are understudied, as are the post-TAVI trajectories of microvascular indices. Aims The aims of this study were to determine the pooled prevalence of CMD, the influence of the diagnostic modality, the post-TAVI coronary flow reserve (CFR) and microvascular resistance changes, and the prognostic impact of baseline CMD on major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with severe aortic stenosis undergoing TAVI. Methods Five databases were searched from January 2010 to December 2025 for studies involving adults with severe aortic stenosis undergoing TAVI in which CMD was assessed by wire-based thermodilution, angiography-derived indices, Doppler measurements, or stress cardiac magnetic resonance. The risk of bias and certainty of evidence were assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and GRADE, respectively. Random-effects meta-analyses (DerSimonian-Laird) pooled CMD prevalence (stratified by modality), CFR change (mean difference; before-after design), and prognostic hazard ratios (HRs). Change in microvascular resistance was synthesized narratively. The protocol was prospectively registered (PROSPERO: CRD42025143775) and reported per the PRISMA 2020 guidance. Results Eleven primary studies were analyzed, 10 of which (n = 1,212) contributed to the prevalence analyses. An additional study (n = 126) was included in the sensitivity analyses only. CMD prevalence was 46.8% (95% confidence interval [CI] [34.0, 59.9]; I2 = 72%) and 38.4% (95% CI [35.3, 41.7]; I2 = 0%) when assessed using wire-based thermodilution (k = 6, n = 324) and angiographic (k = 4, n = 888) indices, respectively. CFR increased post-TAVI by a pooled mean difference of +0.49 (95% CI [+0.27, + 0.71]; I2 = 72%; k = 5, n = 103 paired observations). Reductions in microvascular resistance were confined to pressure-to-velocity and reserve ratio indices, and absolute minimal microvascular resistance was unchanged (k = 4, n = 85). The HR for MACE was 3.22 (95% CI [0.98, 10.60]; I2 = 78%; k = 2, n = 585). Substantial heterogeneity reflected non-equivalent CMD definitions. Conclusion The prevalence of CMD pre-TAVI is influenced by the diagnostic method. CFR tends to improve after TAVI, likely due to reduced resting demand rather than structural repair. The CMD-MACE association should be viewed as hypothesis-generating due to limited studies, varied CMD definitions, and incompatible HR calculations. Prospective multicenter studies with standardized CMD definitions are required.

Reductions in microvascular resistance were confined to pressure-to-velocity and reserve ratio indices, and absolute minimal microvascular resistance was unchanged (k = 4, n = 85). Conclusion

The prevalence of CMD pre-TAVI is influenced by the diagnostic method. CFR tends to improve after TAVI, likely due to reduced resting demand rather than structural repair. The CMD-MACE association should be viewed as hypothesis-generating due to limited studies, varied CMD definitions, and incompatible HR calculations. Prospective multicenter studies with standardized CMD definitions are required.

title: Predicting lymph node metastasis in non-small cell lung cancer using clinical and PET/CT-derived morphological features: An interpretable machine-learning study.
abstract: Background Accurate prediction of lymph node metastasis (LNM) in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is crucial for staging and treatment planning. This study aimed to establish a standardized machine learning workflow based on routinely available clinical, serological, and PET/CT-derived parameters to enhance preoperative LNM risk stratification. Methods This retrospective study included 255 patients with histologically confirmed NSCLC, all of whom underwent systematic lymph-node dissection. Patients were randomly divided, with stratification by pathological lymph-node status, into a training cohort (n = 178) and an internal held-out test test cohort (n = 77). Candidate predictors were screened using univariable and multivariable logistic regression in the training cohort. Six machine-learning algorithms were trained and optimized using repeated nested five-fold cross-validation. After model development was completed, all six models were applied without modification to the test cohort. Test-set AUCs were compared using paired DeLong tests with Holm correction. The primary model was further evaluated for calibration, clinical utility, and feature contribution using SHAP. A conventional multivariable logistic regression model using the same four predictors was added as a simple reference model, and its discrimination and calibration were compared with those of XGBoost. Results Central tumor location, elevated carcinoembryonic antigen, elevated squamous cell carcinoma antigen, and solid nodule status were retained as predictors; none of the quantitative PET metabolic parameters remained independently associated with LNM. XGBoost achieved the highest cross-validated AUC among the six candidate machine-learning algorithms in the training cohort (0.735; 95% CI, 0.653-0.813) and was therefore designated the primary model. In the internal held-out test cohort, XGBoost achieved an AUC of 0.747 (95% CI, 0.631-0.846). The conventional logistic regression reference model achieved a test AUC of 0.733 (95% CI, 0.612-0.841), with no significant difference from XGBoost (DeLong P = 0.301). Its Brier score was 0.152, compared with 0.198 for XGBoost. Conclusion XGBoost model showed moderate discrimination and a high negative predictive value for pathological LNM in NSCLC. However, its limited positive predictive value and the absence of significant differences among the candidate algorithms support cautious interpretation. External multicenter evaluation is required before clinical implementation.

title: A multidisciplinary diagnostic approach to thoracic endometriosis syndrome: Insights from CT imaging, surgery, and pathology.
abstract: Background Thoracic endometriosis syndrome (TES) is the most common extrapelvic manifestation of endometriosis, yet its classification, diagnosis, and treatment remain debated. Thoracic endometriosis syndrome has recently been proposed to be categorized into 3 types: pleural, bronchopulmonary, and diaphragmatic. Objectives Our study aims to propose a 3-step approach - computed tomography (CT) imaging, careful intraoperative assessment, and targeted pathology - to enhance the diagnostic process and optimize the management of TES-related pneumothorax. Material and methods We retrospectively analyzed 3 cases of recurrent right-sided catamenial pneumothorax in female patients with a history of pelvic endometriosis, managed surgically at the Department of Thoracic Surgery, Medical University of Gdansk, between 2021 and 2024. All included patients underwent video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS), with comprehensive preoperative CT imaging, intraoperative lesion mapping, and postoperative histopathological examination, improving diagnostic accuracy in TES, with a possible impact on therapeutic results. Results Chest CT is essential for detecting bullous lesions, aiding in intraoperative identification and surgical treatment. Immunohistochemistry (IHC), assessing estrogen receptor (ER) and CD10 for stromal identification, improves pathological accuracy. Conclusions This study underlines the diagnostic value of integrating imaging, intraoperative assessment, and targeted histopathology, as well as clear communication between surgeons, radiologists, and pathologists to ensure accurate diagnosis and an improved therapeutic process for patients in clinical practice.

title: Biomechanical Evaluation of Uterine Morphology and Tissue Mechanical Properties in a Computational Model of the Pelvic Cavity
abstract: Female pelvic organ prolapse (POP) is a gynecological disorder characterized by pelvic organ descent that significantly impacts quality of life. With increasing global burden, approaches for early diagnosis are essential. This study illustrates a patient-specific computational model of the pelvic cavity, updating the uterine and cervical geometric model and assigning cervical tissue properties. Three distinct uterine geometric models were assembled, based on literature measurements and magnetic resonance images for comparison and validation. Human cervical properties were extrapolated from biomechanical testing of ovine pelvic tissues. Finite elements simulations of the Valsalva maneuver were conducted to analyze the biomechanical effects of varying uterine morphology and tissue properties on the pelvic cavity, including the bladder neck, vagina, and uterosacral ligaments (USLs). Results show that a uterus with softer properties assigned exhibits less vertical displacement and relies more on USLs support than a stiffer one. Furthermore, uterine volume and morphology significantly influence pelvic dynamics: a larger uterus tends toward anteversion, while a smaller uterus increases vertical vaginal displacement (10.57 mm vs 6.04 mm) and requires greater USLs support. Anatomical variations directly constrain bladder neck displacement. These computational advancements aim to enhance patient-specific modeling, assisting clinical decision-making.

title: Prospective Evaluation of Maternal Serum sFlt-1, PlGF, and the sFlt- 1/PlGF Ratio in Placenta Accreta Spectrum and Their Correlation With Placental Immunohistochemical Expression
abstract: Abstract Background Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) is associated with substantial maternal morbidity and mortality, particularly because of severe obstetric haemorrhage. Although antenatal imaging remains the cornerstone of diagnosis, additional biomarkers may have potential value, particularly where access to advanced imaging is limited. This study evaluated maternal serum soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1), placental growth factor (PlGF), and the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio in women with PAS and examined their relationship with placental immunohistochemical expression. Methods This prospective case–control study was conducted at Vardhman Mahavir Medical College and Safdarjung Hospital, New Delhi, in collaboration with the ICMR–National Institute of Pathology. Women with singleton pregnancies beyond 28 weeks with confirmed or clinically diagnosed PAS were enrolled as cases, while age- and gravidity-matched women undergoing caesarean delivery without PAS served as controls. Maternal plasma sFlt-1 and PlGF concentrations were measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Placental tissue was evaluated by histopathology and immunohistochemistry for sFlt-1 and PlGF. Diagnostic performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, and multivariable logistic regression was performed to account for baseline clinical differences. Results Sixty women were included in the final analysis, comprising 40 PAS cases and 20 controls. Median plasma sFlt-1 concentrations were lower in PAS cases than controls (23.5 vs. 29.8 ng/mL; p = 0.034), whereas PlGF concentrations were higher (270.5 vs. 48.2 pg/mL; p = 0.006). The median sFlt-1/PlGF ratio was significantly lower in PAS cases (88.1 vs. 561.1; p = 0.001). ROC analysis demonstrated an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.670 for sFlt-1, 0.716 for PlGF, and 0.753 for the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio. At the selected cut-offs, sFlt-1 showed 100% sensitivity and 65% specificity, PlGF showed 62.5% sensitivity and 100% specificity, and the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio showed 62.5% sensitivity and 95% specificity. None of the three biomarkers differed significantly according to histopathological depth of invasion. In multivariable logistic regression, the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio was not independently associated with PAS after adjustment for maternal age, parity, previous caesarean delivery, and previous placenta previa ( p = 0.110). Placental PlGF immunohistochemical expression showed a significant positive association with plasma PlGF concentration ( p < 0.001), whereas sFlt-1 tissue expression was uniformly weak. Conclusions Maternal plasma sFlt-1, PlGF, and the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio were significantly different in women with PAS compared with controls and demonstrated moderate discriminatory performance. The sFlt-1/PlGF ratio showed the highest AUC among the biomarkers evaluated; however, it was not independently associated with PAS after adjustment for clinical factors. Plasma PlGF correlated significantly with placental PlGF immunohistochemical expression, supporting a biological relationship between circulating and placental PlGF. Larger prospective studies are required to determine whether these biomarkers can provide clinically useful adjunctive information for PAS screening and diagnosis.

title: Detection of the real joint interface between ultrasonically welded aluminium strands (Al-strands) and copper terminals (Cu-terminals) connections using non-destructive testing methods
abstract: Abstract The ongoing electrification of the automotive sector increases the demand for reliable and production-robust electrically conductive joints, particularly in cell interconnection, high-voltage wiring harnesses, and power electronics. Ultrasonic metal welding has become an established joining technology because it forms metallurgical solid-state bonds for material mixes without additional filler materials. At present, the quality of ultrasonically welded joints is assessed primarily by destructive mechanical testing and simple limit value control Although these destructive methods provide reliable information on weld quality, they are limited to sample-based inspection in series production and therefore permit only restricted testing intensity. Consequently, sporadically occurring defects may remain undetected. Against this background, advanced non-destructive testing methods are gaining increasing importance, as they enable the evaluation of joint quality without impairing component functionality and improve diagnostic reliability through a higher inspection frequency. This study investigates various non-destructive testing methods for ultrasonic welded joints between copper terminals and aluminum stranded conductors. The focus lies on quantifying strand compaction by computed tomography and characterizing the effective bonded area using imaging and thermal methods. The findings enable a deeper characterization of the joining zone. Building on these results, the correlation between effective joint area and resulting shear tensile strength is investigated to improve quality prediction by AI-based systems in further studies.

title: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Bone Remodeling of Dysplasia Epiphysealis Hemimelica of the Medial Femoral Condyle in a Child: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Dysplasia epiphysealis hemimelica is a rare osteochondral proliferative lesion in children. It is uncommon when located in the medial femoral condyle, and clinically, it is prone to misdiagnosis. Here, we report a case of a 9-year-old boy who presented with right knee pain and restricted range of motion induced by trauma. Preoperative multimodal imaging, including digital radiography, computed tomography, and magnetic resonance imaging, revealed complex features such as articular cartilage defects, bone marrow edema, and lobulated osseous prominences, requiring differential diagnosis from osteochondritis dissecans and bone tumors. The patient underwent surgical resection of the lesion on the medial femoral condyle of the right femur, and postoperative pathology confirmed the diagnosis of DEH. A 1.5-year post-operative DR follow-up meticulously documented the entire progression of the resected region, transitioning from early bone defect to mid-term bone remodeling, and ultimately to the complete recovery of the anatomical contour in the long term. This case indicates that the integration of multimodal imaging with pathological evaluation facilitates early and precise diagnosis of DEH. For symptomatic pediatric patients with articular involvement, surgical intervention can fully leverage the self-remodeling capacity of pediatric epiphyses, thereby yielding excellent mid- to long-term clinical outcomes.

title: Malnutrition-associated reversible splenial lesion syndrome after metabolic surgery: a case report
abstract: Abstract Background Reversible splenial lesion syndrome (RESLES) is a rare clinicoradiological entity characterized by an oval, reversible lesion in the splenium of the corpus callosum (SCC), with diagnosis relying primarily on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The etiologic spectrum is wide and suggests a “final common pathway” triggered by diverse systemic insults. Metabolic surgery, while effective for weight reduction, can precipitate severe malnutrition and internal environmental perturbations. Here we report a case of RESLES associated with malnutrition after sleeve gastrectomy, which is rarely described in the literature. Case presentation A 14-year-old female with no previous neurological disorders presented with nausea, vomiting, and oliguria one month after undergoing sleeve gastrectomy. Persistent inadequate oral intake post-surgery led to severe malnutrition, dehydration, and acute kidney injury. Laboratory evaluation revealed profound electrolyte disturbances, specifically severe hypokalemia (nadir 2.52 mmol/L), and marked azotemia (creatinine 1451.3 µmol/L). Cranial MRI demonstrated an ovoid lesion (10 × 12 mm) in the SCC with isointensity on T1-weighted images, slight hyperintensity on T2-weighted images, and restricted diffusion on DWI, consistent with RESLES. After one month of intensive treatment—including hemodialysis, fluid resuscitation, electrolyte and vitamin supplementation, and anti-infective therapy—her symptoms resolved completely, and follow-up MRI showed total resolution of the lesion without neurological sequelae. Conclusions Metabolic and osmotic perturbations associated with malnutrition after metabolic surgery may trigger RESLES. Timely identification and correction of the underlying causes yield a favorable prognosis. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for RESLES in post-bariatric patients presenting with neurological symptoms.

title: Neuro-JEPA: Building and Evaluating Health-System Scale Neuroimaging Foundation Models with Mixture of Experts
abstract: Abstract Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain routinely combines complementary contrasts—including T1-weighted (T1w), T2-weighted (T2w) and FLAIR sequences—to capture anatomy and pathology. Although foundation models trained on large neuroimaging datasets have shown promise, it remains unclear whether they effectively integrate these complementary contrasts across diverse clinical settings. Here we present Neuro-JEPA, a multimodal foundation model that learns unified representations across structural brain MRIs. Neuro-JEPA combines latent predictive learning with a sparse Mixture-of-Experts architecture to encode multiple MRI contrasts within a single model. The model is pretrained on 1.55 million scans from 428,647 clinical imaging studies spanning T1w, T2w and FLAIR sequences. The model performance is evaluated on 47 downstream tasks across three independent health systems and 12 public datasets, encompassing single-contrast, multimodal and cross-domain applications. Across these evaluations, Neuro-JEPA achieved the strongest overall performance and generalized robustly across heterogeneous cohorts, outperforming existing neuroimaging foundation models and strong conventional baselines in the majority of comparisons despite using less than one-third of the pretraining data of leading models. Performance gains were particularly pronounced in data-scarce settings, reaching up to 15% over prior foundation models for clinically important pathologies including gliosis and multiple sclerosis. Neuro-JEPA showed clinically relevant capabilities across domains, including prediction of amyloid status and progression from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer’s disease dementia, stroke identification and classification, and prediction of post-stroke functional outcome and length of stay. Together, these results show that data scale, curation and principled model design can act synergistically to produce broadly transferable neuroimaging representations, and establish Neuro-JEPA as a scalable framework toward general-purpose multimodal foundation models for neurological imaging.

Performance gains were particularly pronounced in data-scarce settings, reaching up to 15% over prior foundation models for clinically important pathologies including gliosis and multiple sclerosis. Neuro-JEPA showed clinically relevant capabilities across domains, including prediction of amyloid status and progression from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer’s disease dementia, stroke identification and classification, and prediction of post-stroke functional outcome and length of stay. Together, these results show that data scale, curation and principled model design can act synergistically to produce broadly transferable neuroimaging representations, and establish Neuro-JEPA as a scalable framework toward general-purpose multimodal foundation models for neurological imaging.
